newsitem.title: GERMANY: Exhibition tells history of German Jewish soldiers.
newsitem.headline: Exhibition tells history of German Jewish soldiers.

text.p: An exhibition tracing the curious and conflicting role of Jews in the ranks of the German armed forces over two centuries opened on Monday near Berlin.

The Potsdam exhibition puts special emphasis on the journey of thousands of German Jews from heroic service on the battlefields of World War One to their persecution in the Nazi genocide less than two decades later.
"It may be difficult to bring the images of Jews and German soldiers together," said exhibition curator Frank Naegler.

But he said the purpose of the collection was "to show what role military service had in the integration process of German Jews at the start of the 19th century, and how that is related to their eventual expulsion from German life".
A diary entry from Edwin Landaus, a Jew who was decorated for his service in World War One, describes his reaction to the April 1, 1933 Nazi-enforced boycott of Jewish businesses.
"This country and these people that I until now loved and protected suddenly became my enemy. I was no longer a German, or should no longer be one..I was ashamed to be one of these people."
All non-Aryans were barred from Wehrmacht ranks in World War Two by a 1935 decree from Adolf Hitler.

The experiences portrayed by the exhibition contrast sharply with a report in Monday's London Daily Telegraph which revealed that 77 high-ranking Jewish officers served under Hitler in World War Two, renouncing their religious status in order to retain their posts.
The Telegraph report was based on research by a student working at Cambridge University who interviewed hundreds of former soldiers and their families and examined army files.

The Potsdam exhibition, however, tells the more typical story of Hermann Simpson -- who belatedly received an Iron Cross for valour in World War One from Hitler in 1935. Later, after a period of forced labour under the the Nazis, he was only rescued from threatened execution by the approach of the American army.
After exclusion since the Middle Ages, German Jews were subject to conscription laws starting in 1788.
They played a significant role in the German military during World War One when Jewish community organisations brought 10,000 Jewish volunteers to the ranks of the German army.
But of a German Jewish population which stood at 250,000 in 1939 more than 160,000 were killed in World War Two.
